doc.title: Aebersold Jamey — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Billy Higgins and the Phoenix school program
summary: Cedar Walton's rhythm section, and the week of school clinics where Billy Higgins tuned his own drums, teaching Aebersold to stop complaining about equipment.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: For example, with that one, because you’re focusing on the artist, and he’s playing his music, Cedar Walton: Did he come to you or did you go to him?

No, I went to him. As a matter of fact, they had played an engagement for a week or two before that, and we set this recording up at the end of it so Ron and the drummer would be familiar with the music. Who was it, Billy Higgins?
It was Billy Higgins. I mean...

We did a... I got this school program out in Phoenix, Arizona. Todd Coolman, James Williams and Billy Higgins. We played a week. Each day we’d go to two or three schools. It was about Thursday of the week when it dawned on me that Billy was using school drums everywhere we went, but yet he always sounded the same. Then I realized he had brought his own snare and his cymbals, and when he’d get there, he’d tune everything up the way he wanted it to sound. That taught me a lesson, that drummers feel more comfortable playing with the drums that are tuned the way they like them tuned. And if you have the knowledge to do it, you just do it. You don’t complain about the equipment.

No. It can be even that much more of a reality now, when you’re going on the road, the expense... If you’re flying. If you’re driving, different story. But the expense, and they’re throwing something at you, and you’ve just got to figure out how to make music out of it.
